analysis.one_liner: Raises workplace safety fines, extends OSHA protections to government workers, and strengthens whistleblower rights.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have updated the Occupational Safety and Health Act, the 1970 law that sets federal workplace safety rules. It would have extended those rules to federal, state, and local government employees, raised the maximum fines for serious safety violations from $70,000 to $129,336 (up to $250,000 when a willful violation kills a worker), added prison time for employers whose violations kill or seriously injure workers, protected employees who refuse dangerous work, and given injured workers and families a formal role in safety investigations. It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in dangerous jobs, especially the roughly one in five who work for federal, state, or local governments and are currently outside the federal safety law's coverage. It also helps workers who report injuries or refuse unsafe work, by barring retaliation and adding back pay, reinstatement, and attorney's fees as remedies, and it helps families of workers killed on the job, who would get notification rights and a say before safety citations are settled.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Government employees and workers in unsafe jobs

how_it_helps.text: Extends OSHA safety and health protections to federal, state, and local government employees, a group the current law excludes.

Raises maximum civil penalties from $70,000 to $129,336 for willful or repeated violations, up to $250,000 when such a violation causes a worker's death, and adjusts all penalty amounts for inflation each year.
Increases criminal penalties so an employer whose knowing violation kills a worker can face up to 10 years in prison, and makes officers and directors personally liable.

Strengthens whistleblower rights: protects employees who refuse work they reasonably believe will cause serious injury, bars retaliation for reporting injuries or unsafe conditions, and adds reinstatement, back pay, damages, and attorney's fees as remedies.

Gives injured workers and families of killed workers the right to meet with Labor Department investigators, receive citations at the same time as the employer, and speak before citations are withdrawn or settled.

Requires employers to fix serious, willful, or repeated hazards while a citation is being contested, rather than waiting until appeals finish, and requires Labor to investigate every workplace death and hospitalizing incident.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who violate safety rules — private companies and, for the first time, government agencies themselves. They would face sharply higher fines, daily penalties for uncorrected serious hazards, potential criminal prosecution, and stronger lawsuits from retaliated-against workers. Taxpayers could also bear costs where state and local governments must run OSHA-equivalent programs for their own workers.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies the federal duty to 'any other person performing work at the place of employment,' extending employer liability beyond employees to contractors and other workers on site, which raises compliance costs — particularly for multi-employer construction sites, where a 'site-controlling employer' would have to keep a log of injuries for every worker on site, including other companies' employees.

Small employers are not exempt from the higher penalty floors (a willful or repeated violation causing death carries a minimum $25,000 penalty even for employers with 25 or fewer employees), and businesses would bear costs from inflation-adjusted penalties, daily fines for uncorrected serious hazards, and required electronic injury reporting.

Extending coverage to state and local government workplaces imposes real administrative costs on those governments, which would have up to 36 months to comply but would need new inspection, recordkeeping, and enforcement capacity in states without approved state plans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is higher compliance and penalty costs for employers, including some added costs for small businesses and multi-employer worksites, against materially stronger protections for workers: current OSHA penalties are so low that fines can be cheaper than fixing hazards, and nearly a fifth of the workforce has no federal safety-law coverage at all. The bill includes some small-employer relief on penalty minimums and phased timelines for governments, but it does not cap liability exposure for employers whose workers include contractors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the same day, February 7, 2019, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Courtney introduced the bill on February 7, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup and the House never voted on it, and no Senate companion action appears in the record.
The bill drew 44 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 231 House Democrats, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced the higher penalties, criminal exposure, and expanded liability are better off because the bill never advanced, and so are state and local governments that would have had to cover their own employees under OSHA rules. Workers killed or injured in workplaces outside federal OSHA coverage remain without it.

for.name: Rep. Joe Courtney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the House.

for.name: 44 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republicans cosponsored it.

for.name: Labor unions and workplace safety advocates
for.what_they_did: Longstanding backers of this proposal, which has been introduced in several Congresses as the favored fix to low OSHA penalties and the public-employee coverage gap.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a markup or reported it out, leaving it without a path to the floor.

against.name: Employer and business trade groups
against.what_they_did: Consistently oppose OSHA penalty increases, criminal liability for safety violations, and expanded coverage as costly compliance burdens.

sides.party_line_note: All 44 cosponsors were Democrats (44 of 231 House Democrats) with no Republican support in the record, and the bill never reached a floor vote that would have shown the full partisan split.

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, logging)
industries.note: The bill multiplies their exposure to safety fines (max willful penalty up to $250,000 per violation, plus daily fines for uncorrected serious hazards), criminal prosecution, and multi-employer site liability. Their gain from the bill dying is workers' continued exposure to uncorrected hazards.

The bill would make public agencies subject to OSHA standards, inspections, and penalties for the first time, creating compliance costs for taxpayers — but also safety protections for the roughly one in five workers employed by governments.

industries.industry: Occupational safety compliance and insurance services
industries.note: Stricter recordkeeping, electronic injury reporting, and higher penalty exposure would increase demand for safety consulting and compliance services. This helps employers avoid the very fines the bill creates.
